name: Tyrian Purple
lede: Tyrian purple was the dye of the ancient Mediterranean, drawn a drop at a time from sea snails at Tyre, and for centuries it meant royalty; the deep wine-red on screen is a modern stand-in for a color that ranged from blue to near black.

sections.title: A port, a snail and a word
sections.body:
*Purple* comes from the Latin *purpura*, which in turn comes from the Greek *porphyra*, the name of the dye that classical antiquity made from a Mediterranean sea snail [10]. The color word was named after the dye, not the other way round. Tyre, the dye's most famous port, sits on the coast of southern Lebanon, a short drive south of Beirut [2].

The dye has many names. The Pigment Compendium lists Royal purple, Imperial purple, Purple of the Ancients and Byzantium purple as synonyms, and Paterson adds *whelk red* for the color itself [5][4]. The general color is filed here as [[purple]]; the later imperial shade is [[royal-purple]] and the dusky court color is [[byzantium]].

sections.title: The shellfish
sections.body:
The dye came only from marine snails of the families Muricidae and Thaisidae [5]. Ball names two Mediterranean species, one called *Murex brandaris* and the other *Thais haemastroma*, which Latin writers knew as *purpura* and *buccinum* [1]. Finlay adds *Murex trunculus*, the species he went to Tyre to find [2]. The zoological names used in older books are often out of date, and the Pigment Compendium gives a corrected list of them [5].

The color sits in a gland near the head, which the ancients called the flower or bloom, and which holds a clear fluid [1]. Aristotle describes how it was removed: small snails were broken whole, while on large ones the shell was stripped first [1]. On exposure to sunlight and air the fluid turns from whitish to pale yellow, then green, then blue and finally purple [1].

Greek legend gave the discovery to Hercules, whose dog bit a snail on the beach at Tyre and came away with a stained mouth, though Ball notes that others say the dog's owner was the Phoenician god Melkarth [1][6]. It is a legend. Ball says only that the manufacture was known in Asia Minor from the fifteenth century BC, and that Homer and Virgil mention garments dyed with it [1].

sections.title: How much dye, and how much work
sections.body:
Each snail gave a drop. Garfield says the animals were crushed in autumn and winter, salted for three days and then boiled for ten, and that the dyeing varied from port to port, with water or even honey added to change the shade [6]. A dyer could also combine the fluids of two species: Ball reports that the shade the Romans prized came from mixing them, because the *Murex* extract alone was bright and the Romans wanted a color tinged with black [1].

Books disagree on how many snails a given amount of dye cost, and they use different units. Ball gives about 250,000 shellfish for an ounce of dye [1]. Paterson says it took 60,000 to make half a pint [4]. Gurney, citing the chemist Friedlander's work, gives 12,000 snails for 1.4 grams of pure dye [9]. The three figures cannot be reconciled without knowing what each author meant by dye, so the safe statement is the common one: tens of thousands of animals for a small quantity.

The smell was part of the cost. Ball says the Phoenician dyers were shunned by polite society, that Athens pushed its dye shops to the edge of the city, and that one story blames their use of ammonia from stale urine [1]. Finlay, standing in a modern dye room, says he understood why Tyre had put up with the odor [2]. The shell mounds of the ancient workshops still litter the eastern Mediterranean shore, by Ball's account [1].

sections.title: Worth more than gold
sections.body:
By the third century AD, a pound of purple-dyed wool cost about three times a baker's yearly wage [1]. Ball calls the ancient purple worth more than gold [1]. Gurney reports that the togas of Roman emperors used the dye, and that it took 12,000 mollusks to make 1.4 grams of it [9]. The price explains the rest of the story: purple was the color that told everyone how much you could afford.

Gage observes that true double-dyed Tyrian purple had the rarity value of gold because it was so uneconomical to make, and that the Phoenicians guarded the secret of its manufacture for many centuries [3]. It was also unusually durable [3]. A color that was both rare and lasting was exactly the kind a state would claim.

sections.title: Purple and the law
sections.body:
In Republican Rome the rules were graded: a purple-and-gold robe could be worn only by a triumphant general, and a plain purple one by a general in the field [1]. Senators, consuls and praetors wore broad purple bands at the edges of their togas, and knights and others of similar rank wore narrower ones [1].

Under the emperors the rules tightened. By the fourth century AD only the emperor himself could wear the true purple, and owning cloth dyed with the royal dye, or even with a cheaper imitation, brought heavy penalties [1]. Under Valentinian II, Theodosius and Arcadius, making Tyrian purple outside the imperial dye works was punishable by death [1]. Gage adds that the laws were widely evaded, and that by the fifth century there was a lively black market in purple cloth [3].

The word followed the law. Coles notes that in the Roman Empire *the Purple* meant the emperor himself [10]. Finlay notes the Greek title *Porphyrogenitus*, born in the purple, which signified immense privilege [2].

sections.title: Which purple?
sections.body:
No single swatch captures it. Ball stresses that purple was a fluid concept in antiquity, and that the ancient dye ranged from bluish to deep red depending on how it was prepared and fixed in the cloth [1]. Garfield, reporting an ancient account, says one preparation resembled the sea, the air and a clear sky, which suggests that Tyrian purple was a spectrum from blue to black [6].

The most prized shade was dark. Coles quotes an ancient description of the best purple as the color of clotted blood, dark when seen by reflected light and brilliant when seen against it [10]. Gage adds that Pliny's description was well known in the Middle Ages, and that he compared the finest purple stuffs to the dark rose of an [[gem:amethyst|amethyst]] [3]. By Pliny's own lifetime, Gage notes, a paler purple had become fashionable [3].

Finlay's own search ended in a dye room where he watched a vat produce both a vivid purple as bright as anything Perkin made and a sky blue from the same source [2]. That is the best modern evidence that the ancient color could be much brighter than the deep wine-red we usually draw.

sections.title: The long end of the industry
sections.body:
The dyers disappeared slowly, and the books give different end dates. Paterson says the dye was extracted at Tyre and disappeared in the fifteenth century [4]. Ball ties the loss of the method to the fall of Constantinople to the Turks in 1453 [1]. Finlay finds a possible last mention of purple dyeing as a working industry as early as 1165, when the traveler Benjamin of Tudela recorded that the Jewish community of Thebes was famous for silk and purple [2]. The simplest summary is that the trade shrank over centuries and was gone by the fifteenth.

A scarlet replaced it at the top of the hierarchy. St Clair reports that in 1464 Pope Paul II ordered his cardinals to wear rich scarlet instead of purple, because the snails were nearly extinct by then [8]. The habit stuck, and [[scarlet]] became linked with the Church and the universities [8].

Long before that, painters had found workarounds. In the early Middle Ages a purplish *whelk red* from shellfish on the coasts of England and France was used to dye parchment, but Ball says it was as laborious as the ancient dye and was little used after the eighth century [11]. A lichen dye called folium or archil gave a better color for less effort [11]. Most purples in medieval panel painting were mixed from a blue such as azurite and a red lake [11].

sections.title: Purple without the dye
sections.body:
Because the color carried the meaning, the meaning outlived the dye. In the sixth-century church of San Vitale in Ravenna, the robes of the Emperor Justinian I are made of mosaic stones of an inorganic purple material, and those of the Empress Theodora are purple edged with gold [1]. The same mosaics show Christ in a purple gown, and Ball argues that the later habit of painting Christ's robes in red, crimson or purplish ultramarine drew on the same imperial link [1].

Some imitation purples were openly sold as imitations. The Stockholm papyrus, a collection of ancient dye recipes, contains three for imitation purple dyes [1]. Finlay adds that sixth-century Christian artists used true Tyrian purple for the most precious books, while cheaper documents used cheaper dyes [2].

Later centuries kept borrowing the name. Paterson records that murexide, a synthetic purple made from uric acid in the guano of Peruvian sea birds, was marketed as *Roman purple* in reference to the revered Tyrian [4]. This is the origin of a common error: murexide has nothing to do with snakes, and the story that it came from serpent excrement is a myth. The raw material was bird droppings [4].

sections.title: Rediscovery and chemistry
sections.body:
Ball says the method stayed a mystery for centuries after 1453, until a French zoologist, Felix Henri de Lacaze-Duthiers, rediscovered it in 1856 after seeing a Mediterranean fisherman mark his shirt with a yellow design from a *Thais* snail that then turned purple-red in the sun [1]. The Pigment Compendium records earlier travelers who reported the same behavior in other waters: William Cole on the coasts of Somerset and South Wales in 1683-84, Jussieu on the French Atlantic coast in 1709, Reaumur in Poitou in 1710 and Duhamel in Provence in 1736 [5]. The snails had never entirely vanished; what had gone was the craft.

The chemistry came later. In 1909 the Austrian chemist Friedlander worked out the structure of the colorant and found it almost identical to [[indigo]] [1]. The only difference is a pair of bromine atoms in the places where indigo has hydrogens [1]. The Pigment Compendium gives the main component as 6,6'-dibromoindigotin, and says that two further components, 6-bromoindigotin and 6,6'-dibromoindirubin, were identified only in 1992 [5]. The species *Murex trunculus* also yields indigo and indirubin, which pushes its dye toward blue [5].

That blue is the reason for a surprising modern use. Jewish tradition has its own stake in the question: the sacred blue thread called *tekhelet* is linked to the same shellfish [2]. Finlay describes the dyer John Edmonds testing the idea that, as with woad and [[indigo]], the vat needed its oxygen removed, and that the rotting meat of the snail might do it [2]. Ball is puzzled that shellfish should make such a close cousin of a plant dye, and says the reason is not clear [1]. Today a commercial Tyrian purple from the species *Nucella lapillus* is on sale for artists [5].

sections.title: The name Perkin borrowed
sections.body:
In 1856 an 18-year-old chemist named William Perkin made a dye by accident, and the first name he gave it was Tyrian purple [7][6]. Greenfield describes the color on silk as a shimmering lilac [7]. Finlay suggests Perkin chose the name because it was a legendary description he remembered from learning Latin [2]. Garfield says he chose it to elevate the dye's worth, while his detractors preferred to call it purple sludge [6].

Ball calls the choice canny and wholly inaccurate [1]. Coles says the name was later changed to *mauveine*, and the color is now known as [[mauve]] [10]. Paterson comments that the synthetic purples sold under the old name could not be expected to match the splendor of the original [4]. The Perkin episode revived interest in the older dye; Finlay notes that within four years Napoleon III sent an expedition to find out where Tyre was and what remained of its riches [2].

sections.title: The swatch is not the dye
sections.body:
The swatch on this page, #66023C, is the screen color that Wikipedia lists for Tyrian purple, and it has no ancient pedigree [12]. In the ISCC-NBS naming system it reads as a very deep purplish red [12]. Its nearest named neighbor in our library is [[byzantium]], at a CIEDE2000 distance of 9.4 [12].

Compare that with the history above. The ancient dye ranged from a bluish tone to a deep red, depending on how it was fixed [1]. The deep wine-red of this swatch is a reasonable stand-in for the dark, blood-like end of that range, but it cannot show the vivid purples and the blues that the same snails could produce [1][2].

sections.title: Field notes
sections.body:
We looked for this swatch in 23,781 museum paintings [13]. No painting in our archive carries it on at least five per cent of the canvas within a CIEDE2000 distance of six, as photographed [13]. This describes our archive, not painting as a whole: the photographs are of aged, varnished works, and a color match is not a pigment test [13].

The absence is no surprise. Ball says medieval painters made their purples by mixing azurite with a red lake, and preferred purplish-red lakes to delicate organic extracts [11].

The name itself has lost ground in print. In Google Books, the phrase *Tyrian purple* peaked around 1810, stood at about 34 per cent of that level in 1900 and about 13 per cent in 2000 [14]. The count covers all uses of the phrase, including poetry and the Perkin story [14].

questions.q: Why was Tyrian purple worth more than gold?
choices: Each snail gave only a drop of dye, so the work took tens of thousands of animals
It was mined from a rare stone
It had to be shipped from India
It was banned for most Romans from the start
questions.answer: Each snail gave only a drop of dye, so the work took tens of thousands of animals

questions.q: True or false: Tyrian purple was one fixed shade of deep reddish purple.
What was the first name William Perkin gave to his 1856 dye?

openers: Tyrian purple was chemically a near twin of indigo: the same molecule with two bromine atoms added.
The same snails could give a vivid purple or a sky blue, depending on how the dye was handled.
Perkin's famous mauve was first sold under the name Tyrian purple.
